account: A Mayo Clinic case series published on 31 May 2023 reports that five of six patients with relapsed POEMS syndrome responded to carfilzomib-based regimens. Carfilzomib was therefore already in published use for POEMS before January 2024, although that series did not include the three-drug combination later given to Joseph Coates. In January 2024, Coates, 37, of Renton, Washington, was critically ill with POEMS syndrome. His heart and kidneys were failing, and he was too sick for a stem cell transplant. His partner, Tara Theobald, asked David Fajgenbaum of the University of Pennsylvania and Every Cure for help. Fajgenbaum considered three drugs used for multiple myeloma, a related disease. He recommended carfilzomib, cyclophosphamide, and dexamethasone to Coates’s treating hematologist and oncologist, Wayne Gao, who agreed to administer them. Fajgenbaum later explained, to AAMCNews on 24 September 2024 and in a Penn Medicine video of 17 November 2025, that an early Every Cure algorithm had also scored those drugs highly for POEMS. In February 2025 a brief vignette in The Lancet Haematology described a matching unnamed patient and labeled the result unpublished data. On 20 March 2025 The New York Times reported improvement within a week and transplant eligibility about four months later. Coates later reported that he responded within one or two weeks and left intensive care three weeks later. He reported that he recovered enough to receive a stem cell transplant and reached full remission five months after that transplant. The sources support a contribution from AI alongside the physicians’ judgment. They do not establish the exact model release or isolate its effect on recovery.

ai_role.statement: Fajgenbaum said that he had considered three drugs used for multiple myeloma and that Every Cure’s AI algorithm also scored them highly for POEMS syndrome. In an earlier AAMC interview, he described reviewing the scores and recommending the drugs to Coates’s treating physician. Wayne Gao weighed the risks and administered the treatment. The AI therefore supported the physicians’ assessment of candidate drugs. The sources do not show that it independently devised the regimen or that the benefit would have been impossible without it. The Lancet Haematology commentary contains a brief vignette of a matching unnamed POEMS patient, explicitly labeled unpublished data. No detailed clinical case report, underlying medical records, or case-specific model output was located. The commentary names KGML-xDTD as one of several algorithms in Every Cure’s platform, but it does not establish which algorithm or release was used for Coates.

limitations: No detailed clinical case report, underlying medical records, drug doses, or case-specific model output for Coates was located. The Lancet commentary contains a brief unnamed vignette and explicitly labels the result unpublished data.

display.answer: The case rests on interviews with Coates, Fajgenbaum and Wayne Gao that The New York Times, The New Yorker, AAMCNews and WHYY report. Every Cure, Penn Medicine and the Advanced Research Projects Agency for Health later describe the same treatment, and Every Cure's investigators wrote the Lancet Haematology commentary. These accounts share witnesses and investigators, and none of them gives independent clinical confirmation. The Mayo Clinic case series of 31 May 2023 concerns other patients and gives context only.

data.chronology_note: The case date remains March 20, 2025, the NYT publication date recorded for this entry. Earlier reporting is preserved here without substituting a different date in this revision.

claim_chains.finding: The NYT article, its archived English copy, and the licensed Infobae translation are one reporting origin. The original includes testimony from Coates and Wayne Gao. The New Yorker has its own interview. Penn Medicine adds original patient and partner testimony and earlier patient videos. AAMC and WHYY add earlier interviews with Fajgenbaum. The Lancet commentary gives a brief vignette labeled unpublished data. These sources are original accounts, but their shared witnesses and institutional relationships do not constitute independent clinical replication.

Fajgenbaum says in the documentary that he had considered the drugs and that AI also scored them highly. His September 2024 AAMC interview describes reviewing the scores before recommending drugs and explicitly dates Joseph’s crisis to January. WHYY’s March 2024 account describes a matching unnamed Washington patient about six weeks after the appeal. These accounts support AI-assisted assessment alongside clinical judgment, not the claim that AI alone invented an untested regimen.

Every Cure identifies an early version of its algorithms for the January 2024 treatment. A January 30 interview describes multiple algorithms, including Elsevier contributions, without identifying which produced Coates’s scores. WHYY names MATRIX in March 2024. Neither that platform name nor the later KGML-xDTD documentation establishes the algorithm or release used for Coates.

claim_chains.claim: Treatment novelty and the separate summer-2024 conference report
claim_chains.finding: A 2021 JACC case report describes the same three drugs for a different POEMS patient. EHA abstract PB2758 reports a separate eight-patient Qilu Hospital cohort, with seven responses. Neither source reports AI involvement. The EHA abstract is a plausible match for Every Cure’s uncited conference reference, but that match remains an inference. Both are clinical context, not evidence about Coates or independent verification of his AI-assisted recommendation.

contextual_clinical_precedents.finding: A different 66-year-old patient treated at Oregon Health & Science University received carfilzomib, cyclophosphamide, and dexamethasone for POEMS syndrome. This establishes clinical use before Coates’s treatment. No AI contribution is described.
contextual_clinical_precedents.relationship: Contextual clinical precedent only. Not retained as evidence of Coates’s outcome and not counted toward confidence in this case.

contextual_clinical_precedents.finding: A retrospective Qilu Hospital cohort included eight POEMS patients treated from March 2022 through January 2024. Seven responded, and one underwent autologous stem cell transplantation. These are other patients, and no AI involvement is stated.

contextual_clinical_precedents.relationship: Plausible match for Every Cure’s summer-2024 conference claim, but the portfolio does not cite PB2758, so the match remains inferential. Context only, not counted as evidence of Coates’s treatment or of AI’s benefit.

fields.account: A Mayo Clinic case series published on 31 May 2023 reports that five of six patients with relapsed POEMS syndrome responded to carfilzomib-based regimens. Carfilzomib was therefore already in published use for POEMS before January 2024, although that series did not include the three-drug combination later given to Joseph Coates. In January 2024, Coates, 37, of Renton, Washington, was critically ill with POEMS syndrome. His heart and kidneys were failing, and he was too sick for a stem cell transplant. His partner, Tara Theobald, asked David Fajgenbaum of the University of Pennsylvania and Every Cure for help. Fajgenbaum considered three drugs used for multiple myeloma, a related disease. He recommended carfilzomib, cyclophosphamide, and dexamethasone to Coates’s treating hematologist and oncologist, Wayne Gao, who agreed to administer them. Fajgenbaum later explained, to AAMCNews on 24 September 2024 and in a Penn Medicine video of 17 November 2025, that an early Every Cure algorithm had also scored those drugs highly for POEMS. In February 2025 a brief vignette in The Lancet Haematology described a matching unnamed patient and labeled the result unpublished data. On 20 March 2025 The New York Times reported improvement within a week and transplant eligibility about four months later. Coates later reported that he responded within one or two weeks and left intensive care three weeks later. He reported that he recovered enough to receive a stem cell transplant and reached full remission five months after that transplant. The sources support a contribution from AI alongside the physicians’ judgment. They do not establish the exact model release or isolate its effect on recovery.

produced_by: Fajgenbaum recognized similarities between POEMS syndrome and multiple myeloma and reviewed high AI scores for drugs that were used for myeloma.
Fajgenbaum answered the family’s urgent appeal and discussed treatment with Wayne Gao, who assessed the risks and administered the three drugs.

purpose: Every Cure uses AI to rank existing drugs as candidates for other diseases. Its early algorithms helped Fajgenbaum assess drugs that he had considered for Coates’s POEMS syndrome. The New Yorker notes that Every Cure does not usually make recommendations for individual patients.

ratings.reason: Coates was critically ill, too sick for a transplant, and facing hospice care. He reported that he began responding to the drug regimen within one or two weeks, later received a stem cell transplant, and reached full remission five months after that transplant. The reported benefit was life-preserving. The available evidence does not isolate AI’s contribution from clinical judgment, the drugs, supportive care, or the transplant.
